claim: After few seconds of adaptation by finger-tapping, the perceived numerosity of spatial arrays and temporal sequences of visual objects displayed near the tapping region is increased or decreased.
source: We have previously shown that after few seconds of adaptation by finger-tapping, the perceived numerosity of spatial arrays and temporal sequences of visual objects displayed near the tapping region is increased or decreased, implying the existence of a sensorimotor numerosity system (Anobile et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Anobile et al., 2016

claim: A sensorimotor numerosity system exists.
source: We have previously shown that after few seconds of adaptation by finger-tapping, the perceived numerosity of spatial arrays and temporal sequences of visual objects displayed near the tapping region is increased or decreased, implying the existence of a sensorimotor numerosity system (Anobile et al., 2016).
evidence: Inferred from adaptation effects and supported by citation

claim: High positive correlations for nearby target numbers were found, scaling down with numerical distance.
source: The results showed high positive correlations for nearby target numbers, scaling down with numerical distance, implying tuning selectivity.
evidence: Reported as experimental result from the current study

claim: Factor analysis identified two factors, one for low and the other for higher numbers.
source: Factor analysis identified two factors, one for low and the other for higher numbers.
evidence: Reported as result from factor analysis in the current study

claim: Principal component analysis revealed two bell-shaped covariance channels, peaking at different numerical values.
source: Principal component analysis revealed two bell-shaped covariance channels, peaking at different numerical values.
evidence: Reported as result from PCA in the current study

claim: Non-numerical strategies based on tapping frequency and response duration do not account for the results.
source: Two control experiments ruled out the role of non-numerical strategies based on tapping frequency and response duration.
evidence: Reported as result from control experiments in the current study

claim: At least two sensorimotor number channels exist that are responsible for translating symbolic numbers into action sequences.
source: These results reinforce our previous reports based on adaptation, and further suggest the existence of at least two sensorimotor number channels responsible for translating symbolic numbers into action sequences.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental results of the current study

claim: Humans share with many animals a primitive non-verbal number system encoding the number of objects in space and events in time.
source: Humans share with many animals a primitive non-verbal number system encoding the number of objects in space and events in time (Dehaene, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dehaene, 2011

claim: The capacity to estimate number rapidly but imperfectly is thought to be a primary perceptual attribute, often termed the number sense.
source: The capacity to estimate number rapidly but imperfectly is thought to be a primary perceptual attribute, often termed the number sense (Burr and Ross, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Burr and Ross, 2008

claim: The sense of number is truly general, transcending space and time, as well as modality and format.
source: Many studies show that the sense of number is truly general, transcending space and time, as well as modality and format (Arrighi et al., 2014; Burr et al., 2017; Togoli et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Numerosity has been shown to interact strongly with action.
source: More recently, numerosity has been shown to interact strongly with action, leading to the idea of a sensorimotor number system, incorporating action, and its interaction with sensory systems (Anobile et al., 2016; Anobile et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Anobile et al., 2016 and 2021

claim: Adaptation to fast tapping causes underestimation of numerosity and slow tapping causes overestimation.
source: participants first tap continuously with their index finger for a few seconds, either rapidly or slowly, then estimate the numerosity of a dot array presented near the adapted region: adaptation to fast tapping causes underestimation and slow tapping overestimation (Anobile et al., 2016; Anobile et al., 2020; Maldonado Moscoso et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple adaptation studies

claim: Motor adaptation induces similar effects on sequential visual and auditory stimuli.
source: Motor adaptation induces similar effects on sequential visual and auditory stimuli (Anobile et al., 2016; Togoli et al., 2020), consistent with the existence of a generalized system linking motor and sensory signals to encode numerosity (Anobile et al., 2021; Burr et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Anobile et al., 2016 and Togoli et al., 2020

claim: Neurons in the posterior parietal cortex of monkeys showed selectivity to the number of self-generated actions, whatever the action.
source: In a seminal paper, Sawamura et al., 2002 trained monkeys to repetitively make five identical movements, then switch to a different movement, in a cyclical fashion: neurons in the posterior parietal cortex showed selectivity to the number of self-generated actions, whatever the action.
evidence: Supported by citation to Sawamura et al., 2002

claim: Neurons in the crow telencephalon were shown to be tuned to the impending number of self-generated actions during the phase between the disappearance of the target to the onset of motor reproduction.
source: Kirschhock and Nieder, 2022 trained crows to peck a specific number of times (1–5). Neurons in the telencephalon were shown to be tuned to the impending number of self-generated actions, during the phase between the disappearance of the target to the onset of motor reproduction.
evidence: Supported by citation to Kirschhock and Nieder, 2022

claim: The activity of neurons in crow telencephalon predicted the behavioral performance and was independent of both stimulus format (dots or digits) and of the temporal characteristics of the motor responses.
source: The activity of these neurons predicted the behavioral performance and was independent of both stimulus format (dots or digits) and of the temporal characteristics of the motor responses.
evidence: Supported by citation to Kirschhock and Nieder, 2022 in the preceding context

claim: Each tuning function of neurons in crow telencephalon peaked at a given preferred numerosity, with activity scaling down with numerical distance.
source: Each tuning function peaked at a given preferred numerosity, with activity scaling down with numerical distance.
evidence: Supported by citation to Kirschhock and Nieder, 2022 in the preceding context

claim: The interindividual covariance technique has been widely used to reveal visual channels for motion, spatial frequency, contrast sensitivity, color, and duration.
source: This technique has been widely used to reveal visual channels for motion (Morrone et al., 1999), spatial frequency (Reynaud and Hess, 2017; Simpson and McFadden, 2005), contrast sensitivity (Peterzell et al., 1995; Peterzell and Teller, 1996), color (Peterzell et al., 2000; Peterzell and Teller, 2000), and duration (Rammsayer and Troche, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Performance measures of stimuli detected by the same mechanism should correlate more between individuals than stimuli detected by different mechanisms.
source: The rationale behind this technique is that performance measures of stimuli detected by the same mechanism should correlate more between individuals than stimuli detected by different mechanisms.
evidence: Based on established principles of the covariance technique

claim: Thirty participants took part in the fast-tapping condition.
source: Thirty participants took part in the fast-tapping condition (age: average = 25.75, SD = 4.5, min = 18, max = 39)
evidence: Reported as methodological detail

claim: Twenty-nine participants took part in the slow tapping condition.
source: 29 in the slow tapping condition (age: average = 25.43, SD = 4.04, min = 18, max = 39)
evidence: Reported as methodological detail

claim: Eighteen participants completed both fast and slow tapping conditions.
source: Of these, 18 completed both conditions.
evidence: Reported as methodological detail

claim: Serial counting was prevented by vocal suppression, repeating aloud the syllable 'ba'.
source: Following previous studies (Cordes et al., 2001; Whalen et al., 1999), serial counting was prevented by vocal suppression, repeating aloud the syllable 'ba' (as fast as possible).
evidence: Reported as methodological procedure with supporting citations

claim: The rate of tapping was higher in the fast tapping (average = 6.8 Hz, SD = 1) compared with the slow tapping condition (average = 3.3 Hz, SD = 1.6).
source: As expected, the rate of tapping was higher in the fast tapping (average = 6.8 Hz, SD = 1) compared with the slow tapping condition (average = 3.3 Hz, SD = 1.6).
evidence: Reported as experimental result

claim: Participants were able to correctly perform the numerical matching task, with average number of reproduced actions scaling linearly with visual targets (both r=0.99).
source: In both conditions, participants were able to correctly perform the numerical matching task, with average number of reproduced actions scaling linearly with visual targets (both r=0.99, Figure 2A, C).
evidence: Reported as experimental result with reference to Figure 2A, C

claim: Average Weber fractions in the fast and slow conditions were virtually identical (average = 0.17).
source: Average Wfs (across target number) in the fast and slow conditions were virtually identical (average = 0.17, SD = 0.01 and average = 0.17, SD = 0.007 for fast and slow tapping respectively)
evidence: Reported as experimental result

claim: Within each condition, Weber fractions were roughly constant across targets, following Weber's Law.
source: within each condition, Wfs were roughly constant across targets, following Weber's Law.
evidence: Reported as experimental result

claim: The correlations of Weber fractions across participants were all positive, ranging from 0.1 to 0.75 in the fast condition and 0.3–0.88 in the slow condition.
source: The correlations were all positive, ranging from 0.1 to 0.75 in the fast condition and 0.3–0.88 in the slow condition.
evidence: Reported as experimental result

claim: Higher correlations lie near the diagonal of the correlation matrix, indicating that motor matching performance was more similar for neighboring numbers compared to higher numerical distance.
source: Importantly, the correlations were clearly not randomly distributed, but most of the higher correlations (reddish) lie near the diagonal, indicating that the motor matching performance was more similar for neighboring numbers, compared to higher numerical distance.
evidence: Reported as experimental result with reference to Figure 3A, C

claim: There is a systematic decreasing trend in correlation coefficients as a function of numerical distance in both fast and slow tapping conditions.
source: There is a systematic decreasing trend in both fast and slow tapping conditions (linear fit on unbinned data shown by dashed lines in Figure 3B, D: slopes = –0.58±0.11,–0.57±0.07 for fast and slow respectively, both p<0.001)
evidence: Reported as experimental result with statistical analysis and reference to Figure 3B, D

claim: The degree of performance similarity was systematically modulated by the numerical difference between targets, in line with the existence of underlying tuning functions.
source: Overall, these analyses confirm that the degree of performance similarity was systematically modulated by the numerical difference between targets, in line with the existence of underlying tuning functions.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental results

claim: The fits with a single channel model were very poor, with R2=0.003 and 0.002 for the fast and slow tapping respectively.
source: The fits with a single channel were very poor, with R2=0.003 and 0.002 (essentially no better than the mean) for the fast and slow tapping respectively.
evidence: Reported as modeling result

claim: The two-channel model gave much better fits, with R2=0.54 and 0.29.
source: However, the two-channel model gave much better fits, with R2=0.54 and 0.29.
evidence: Reported as modeling result

claim: The four-channel model had similarly good fits, with R2=0.52 and 0.28.
source: The four-channel model had similarly good fits, with R2=0.52 and 0.28.
evidence: Reported as modeling result

claim: Hierarchical clustering analysis returned a two-cluster solution with one cluster aggregating low numbers (N8-13 and N8-14 in the fast and slow conditions) and the other aggregating high numbers (N>13 and N>14, respectively).
source: In both the fast and slow tapping conditions, the analyses returned a two-cluster solution with one cluster aggregating low numbers (N8-13 and N8-14 in the fast and slow conditions) and the other aggregating high numbers (N>13 and N>14, respectively).
evidence: Reported as result from hierarchical clustering analysis

claim: Control analysis on randomised data yielded clusters containing contiguous numbers only in 0.005% of cases for both the fast and slow tapping conditions.
source: A control analysis on randomised data (see Methods) yielded clusters containing contiguous numbers only in 0.005% of cases (for both the fast and slow tapping conditions), suggesting that the results with the original dataset likely represent a structure genuinely organised as a function of the highest similarity between neighboring numbers.
evidence: Reported as result from control analysis

claim: Factor analysis revealed two factors explaining a total of 68% and 81% of the total variance for the fast and slow tapping conditions, respectively.
source: In both fast and slow tapping conditions, two factors emerged (see Methods), explaining a total of 68% and 81% of the total variance (for the fast and slow tapping conditions, respectively).
evidence: Reported as result from factor analysis

claim: The results revealed two bell-shaped tuning functions for both fast and slow tapping conditions, with factor strength distributions reasonably described by logGaussian functions.
source: The results revealed two bell-shaped tuning functions for both fast (panel B) and slow (panel D) tapping conditions, with factor strength distributions reasonably described by logGaussian functions (fast tapping: R2=0.6 and R2=0.65; slow tapping: R2=0.97, R2=0.94 for 1st and 2nd components).
evidence: Reported as result from factor analysis with reference to Figure 4

claim: In the fast-tapping condition, the first component peaked at lower target numbers (N 11) and the second component at higher numbers (N 29).
source: In the fast-tapping condition, the first component peaked at lower target numbers (N 11) and the second component at higher numbers (N 29).
evidence: Reported as result from factor analysis

claim: In the slow motor condition, the first component peaked at higher target numbers (N 26) and the second component at lower numbers (N 8).
source: In the slow motor condition, the first component packed at higher target numbers (N 26) and the second component at lower numbers (N 8).
evidence: Reported as result from factor analysis

claim: Total response duration was positively correlated with target numbers (r=0.95, r=0.36, for fast and slow tapping, both p<0.001).
source: However, as total response duration was positively correlated with target numbers (r=0.95, r=0.36, for fast and slow tapping, both p<0.001), participants might have used response duration instead of number of taps as a stop criterion.
evidence: Reported as experimental result

claim: The precision level (Weber fractions) in the number task was clearly lower (higher precision) than the duration task.
source: Figure 5A, B shows that this was not the case with the precision level (Wfs) in the number task being clearly lower (higher precision) than the duration task, making the use of duration strategies during the number task unlikely (number: average = 0.16, SD = 0.03; duration: average = 0.24, SD = 0.04).
evidence: Reported as experimental result with reference to Figure 5A, B

claim: A repeated measures ANOVA confirmed the difference in Weber fractions between number and duration tasks (F(1, 80) = 19.97, p=0.002).
source: A RM ANOVA with task (duration, number) and stimuli intensity (11 levels) confirmed the difference (F(1, 80) = 19.97, p=0.002).
evidence: Reported as statistical analysis result

claim: Precision in number reproduction followed Weber's law, a well-established signature of the Approximate Number System.
source: Replicating previous evidence from both human and animal studies (Cordes et al., 2001; Kirschhock and Nieder, 2022; Whalen et al., 1999), precision followed Weber's law, a well-established signature of the Approximate Number System (Anobile et al., 2014; Dehaene, 2011; Feigenson et al., 2004; Ross, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Digits encoding, at least with educated adults, is noiseless.
source: Digits encoding, at least with educated adults, is noiseless, eliminating this source of variability but leaving that associated with the sensorimotor transformation process.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about digit processing in adults

claim: The covariance technique is based on the idea that interindividual variability conveys information that can reveal common sensory processes.
source: The technique is based on the idea that interindividual variability conveys information that can reveal common sensory processes (Peterzell and Kennedy, 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to Peterzell and Kennedy, 2016

claim: Regions of high intercorrelation between neighboring stimuli intensity can be interpreted to imply that sets of stimuli are processed by the same (shared) underlying channel.
source: Regions of high intercorrelation between neighboring stimuli intensity can be interpreted to imply that sets of stimuli are processed by the same (shared) underlying channel.
evidence: Based on principles of the covariance technique

claim: Relatively lower correlations among more distant stimuli would indicate that these are processed by different, or at least partially independent, channels.
source: Following this rationale, relatively lower correlations among more distant stimuli would indicate that these are processed by different, or at least partially independent, channels (Peterzell and Teller, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to Peterzell and Teller, 1996

claim: The results obtained in this study are in line with those predicted by the covariance technique, implying the existence of sensorimotor channels tuned to different numerical targets.
source: The results obtained in this study are in line with those predicted by this technique, implying the existence of sensorimotor channels tuned to different numerical targets, with a rather wide response distribution.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental results

claim: The sensorimotor channels probably reflect the activity of noisy neurons responsible for translating sensory information into the corresponding numerical motor output, such as those observed in crows.
source: These channels probably reflect the activity of noisy neurons responsible for translating sensory information into the corresponding numerical motor output, such as those observed in crows (Kirschhock and Nieder, 2022).
evidence: Speculative interpretation with supporting citation

claim: The results reinforce adaptation studies showing number-selective adaptation between actions and perceived numerosity.
source: The results reinforce adaptation studies showing number-selective adaptation between actions and perceived numerosity (Anobile et al., 2016; Maldonado Moscoso et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to adaptation studies

claim: The results are broadly in line with recent evidence from animal physiology showing number selective sensorimotor neurons in the crow brain.
source: The results are also broadly in line with recent evidence from animal physiology showing number selective sensorimotor neurons in the crow brain, translating visual inputs (digits and dot arrays) into number of pecks (Kirschhock and Nieder, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kirschhock and Nieder, 2022

claim: The crow study found as many channels as the number tested (N1–5).
source: While the crow study found as many channels as the number tested (N1–5), we found evidence for only two channels (clusters and factors) over the range of 8–32.
evidence: Supported by citation to Kirschhock and Nieder, 2022 in the preceding context

claim: PCA aims to summarize the dataset with the minimal number of components (channels).
source: However, it is important to note that PCA aims to summarize the dataset with the minimal number of components (channels).
evidence: Based on established knowledge about PCA methodology

claim: The existence of more than two (perhaps not fully independent) channels cannot be excluded.
source: We can therefore not exclude the possible existence of more than two (perhaps not fully independent) channels.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the results

claim: The results should not be interpreted as evidence for only two sensorimotor channels, but rather as evidence that tuned mechanisms exist in the human brain, with at least two different tunings.
source: The results should be not interpreted as evidence for only two sensorimotor channels, but rather as evidence that tuned mechanisms exist in the human brain, with at least two different tunings.
evidence: Interpretation of the experimental results

claim: The predictions of two or multiple channels are very similar, difficult to distinguish with the current technique.
source: This is also apparent from the simulations of Figure 1, showing that the predictions of two or multiple channels are very similar, difficult to distinguish with the current technique.
evidence: Based on simulations shown in Figure 1

claim: The fits to the data using two or four channels were very similar, but both almost infinitely better than the one-channel fit.
source: Indeed, the fits to the data using two or four channels were very similar, but both almost infinitely better than the one-channel fit.
evidence: Reported as modeling result

claim: The channels described here likely represent a coarse summary representation of several (probably sharper) underlying channels.
source: In other words, the channels described here likely represent a coarse summary representation of several (probably sharper) underlying channels.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the results

claim: The results reported here are unlikely to be contaminated by strategies capitalizing on duration of motor responses and/or temporal frequency.
source: The results reported here are unlikely to be contaminated by strategies capitalizing on duration of motor responses and/or temporal frequency.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental results

claim: For fast actions lower number targets show more variance than higher numbers, and vice versa for slower actions.
source: This result suggests that for fast actions lower number targets show more variance than higher numbers, and vice versa for slower actions.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental results

claim: Duration could conceivably be useful proxy for numerosity, but only if the thresholds for duration were lower than those for numerosity.
source: Duration could conceivably be useful proxy for numerosity, but only if the thresholds for duration were lower than those for numerosity: but the results show they are in fact higher.
evidence: Logical inference from the experimental results

claim: Previous studies showed lower sensitivities for motor matching duration tasks compared with motor number matching tasks.
source: Once again, these results are in line with previous studies showing lower sensitivities for motor matching duration tasks compared with motor number matching tasks.
evidence: Supported by reference to previous studies

claim: The electrophysiological study on crows found similar neural response curves across very different motor response timing conditions.
source: The electrophysiological study on crows also found similar neural response curves across very different motor response timing conditions (Kirschhock and Nieder, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kirschhock and Nieder, 2022

claim: The channels found here reflect a genuine number selective sensorimotor transformation process.
source: In summary, the results seem to suggest that the channels found here, like those in crows, reflect a genuine number selective sensorimotor transformation processes.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental results

claim: Desert ants rely on the number of steps to return to the nest.
source: For example, desert ants rely on the number of steps to return to the nest (Wittlinger et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by citation to Wittlinger et al., 2006

claim: Some species of male frogs match or exceed the chucks of competitors to attract female partner.
source: some species of male frogs match or exceed the chucks of competitors to attract female partner (Rose, 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to Rose, 2017

claim: Some songbirds modulate the numbers of syllables in their calls to signal dangerousness of predators.
source: some songbirds modulate the numbers of syllables in their calls to signal dangerousness of predators (Suzuki, 2016; Templeton et al., 2005)
evidence: Supported by citations to Suzuki, 2016 and Templeton et al., 2005

claim: The use of number-related motor strategies by animals has a clear ecological value for survival and species preservation.
source: In all cases, the use of number-related motor strategies by animals has a clear ecological value for survival and species preservation.
evidence: Inferred from the examples provided

claim: The sensorimotor number system may have been preserved in humans and repurposed for our species-specific needs.
source: This system may have been preserved in humans and repurposed for our species-specific needs.
evidence: Speculative interpretation

claim: In humans numerosity estimation may act as a non-symbolic precursor for the development of symbolic mathematical skills.
source: Although most animal species are capable of some form of numerosity estimation (Butterworth, 2022), it appears that in humans numerosity estimation may act as a non-symbolic precursor for the development of symbolic mathematical skills (Chen and Li, 2014; Decarli et al., 2023; Halberda et al., 2008; Mazzocco et al., 2011; Piazza, 2010; Piazza et al., 2010; Schneider et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: The sensorimotor system could act as an early tool to constantly update and calibrate motor and sensory systems for the encoding and active manipulation of quantities and objects.
source: The sensorimotor system could act as an early tool to constantly update and calibrate motor and sensory systems for the encoding and active manipulation of quantities and objects, with a potential impact on the quality of formal mathematical skills in later development.
evidence: Speculative interpretation

claim: There are reports of a possible co-occurrence of motor impairments in children with mathematical learning disorders such as dyscalculia.
source: In line with this idea, there are reports of a possible co-occurrence of motor impairments in children with mathematical learning disorders such as dyscalculia (Westendorp et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citation to Westendorp et al., 2011

claim: Children with developmental coordination disorders (which impair gross and fine motor function) perform poorly on math and numerosity tasks.
source: children with developmental coordination disorders (which impair gross and fine motor function) perform poorly on math and numerosity tasks (Gomez et al., 2015; Gomez et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to Gomez et al., 2015 and 2017

claim: Walsh proposed a sensory magnitude system, encoding abstract quantities such as space, time and number, to guide planning and execution of actions.
source: This is in line with the suggestive idea proposed by Walsh, 2003 of a sensory magnitude system, encoding abstract quantities such as space, time and number, to guide planning and execution of actions.
evidence: Supported by citation to Walsh, 2003

claim: The acquisition of number meaning is deeply grounded in sensorimotor experiences.
source: It is also in line with more recent proposal suggesting that the acquisition of number meaning is deeply grounded in sensorimotor experiences (Ranzini et al., 2022; Sixtus et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ranzini et al., 2022 and Sixtus et al., 2023

claim: This is the first study showing sensorimotor channels for the transformation of numbers into action sequences in humans.
source: This is the first study showing sensorimotor channels for the transformation of numbers into action sequences in humans, and many questions remain open.
evidence: Claimed as novel contribution of the current study
